title: Degenerate four-wave mixing in a CPT-symmetric coupler with intermodal dispersion
authors: Nguyen Duc Anh Quan, Do Duc Tho, Marek Trippenbach, Nguyen Thi Dung, Tran Thi Hai, Nguyen Viet Hung
abstract: Four-wave mixing provides a simple setting in which dispersion, nonlinearity, and non-Hermiticity compete to select resonant energy-transfer channels. We study degenerate four-wave mixing in a Kerr dual-core coupler with balanced gain and loss and frequency-dependent intercore coupling. The dispersive coupling changes the symmetry from conventional $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry to a combined $\mathcal{CPT}$ symmetry and reshapes the two-branch linear spectrum. We determine the unbroken-$\mathcal{CPT}$ domain and classify the branch configurations that can satisfy the degenerate phase-matching condition. In the parameter ranges examined, three resonant channels persist over broad regions, whereas a same-branch channel appears only close to the symmetry-breaking threshold. In this near-threshold regime, a single pump can simultaneously satisfy two distinct nonzero sideband resonances. Direct pulse simulations confirm the predicted resonances and reveal secondary-wave generation and multifrequency cascades near eigenmode coalescence. A reduced three-wave model captures the initial dynamics away from the exceptional point but loses accuracy as the modal basis becomes ill-conditioned. These results show how dispersive coupling reorganizes resonances, group-velocity mismatch, and nonlinear energy exchange in a non-Hermitian wave system, and they identify the exceptional-point region as a regime where a few-mode description can break down.
summary: This paper studies degenerate four-wave mixing in a CPT-symmetric optical coupler that includes intermodal dispersion. The authors analyze how this dispersive coupling reorganizes nonlinear resonances by determining conditions for phase-matching within the system's non-Hermitian spectrum. Key findings include identifying stable resonant channels and demonstrating complex wave dynamics, particularly near spectral singularities where simple theoretical models break down.
main_problem: The study investigates how competing effects—dispersion, nonlinearity, and non-Hermiticity—select resonant energy-transfer channels during degenerate four-wave mixing (FWM). The focus is on the reorganization of resonances due to dispersive coupling in a CPT-symmetric system.
main_result: The analysis shows that three resonant channels persist over broad parameter regions, and near symmetry-breaking thresholds, a single pump can simultaneously support two distinct sideband resonances. Dispersive coupling fundamentally reorganizes energy exchange mechanisms in this non-Hermitian wave system.
method: The research combines analytical methods to solve the degenerate phase-matching condition within the unbroken-CPT domain with direct pulse simulations to confirm predicted resonance structures and secondary wave generation.
model_or_system: The model is a Kerr dual-core coupler governed by coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations, incorporating balanced gain/loss ($\pm i\gamma$) and frequency-dependent intercore coupling ($K$). The system's dynamics are characterized by CPT symmetry.
key_observables: Resonant energy-transfer channels, the output FWM spectral fraction ($\eta_{FWM}$), and secondary wave generation/multifrequency cascades near eigenmode coalescence.
important_parameters: The Kerr coefficient ($\sigma$), coupling dispersion coefficients ($\kappa_0, \kappa_1, \kappa_2$), and operating regimes near exceptional points or symmetry-breaking thresholds.
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes a weak-to-moderate coupling-dispersion regime (perturbative) and that the reduced three-wave model remains accurate, though this fails near exceptional points.
figures_summary: Figures likely map out $\eta_{FWM}$ in parameter planes ($\kappa_1, \kappa_2$), delineating regions of unbroken vs. broken spectrum, and illustrating resonance existence across different coupling configurations (I, II, IV).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model and symmetry (CPT), analyzes the linear spectrum to define the unbroken domain, derives algebraic conditions for degenerate phase-matching, classifies possible resonant branch triples, and finally uses simulations/diagnostics to confirm complex nonlinear dynamics near critical points.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it models energy transfer in a non-Hermitian setting where spectral singularities (exceptional points) dictate the breakdown of simple few-mode approximations, which is crucial for understanding realistic photonic devices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Linear dispersion relations for {κ0, κ1, κ2} = {1, 0.3, 0.04}. (a) Unbroken CPT phase at γ = 0.4. (b) Broken phase at γ = 0.5 > γCPT = 0.4375. The shaded interval marks frequencies for which the branches coalesce and the propagation constants form a complex-conjugate pair.

FIG. 2. Graphical solutions of Eq. (12). (a) Configurations (I)–(III) for {κ0, κ1, κ2} = {1, 0.3, 0.04}, γ = 0.4, and ωp = 2.3. (b) The same three branch combinations at γ = γCPT = 0.4375 and ωp = −3.38. The blue dashed curves are the left-hand side and the solid curves are the configuration-dependent right-hand sides. (c) Zero contours for configuration (IV) with {κ0, κ1, κ2} = {1, 0.01, 0.6} and γ = γCPT −10−5. The green line is the trivial root δ = 0 and the cyan curves are nonzero solutions. At ωp = −0.3 (red dashed line), two positive roots and their negative counterparts coexist. The black dashed line marks ω∗= −κ1/(2κ2).

FIG. 3. Group velocities of the phase-matched waves as functions of ωp. (a) Configuration (I). (b) Configurations (II) and (III), shown by solid and dashed blue curves. Panels (a) and (b) use {γ, κ1, κ2} = {0.4, 0.3, 0.04}. (c) Configuration (IV) for {γ, κ1, κ2} = {γCPT −10−5, 0.01, 0.6}. Red curves represent the pump branch and blue curves the generated sidebands. Crossings indicate exact group-velocity matching; nearby regions provide long but finite pulse overlap.

FIG. 4. Configuration (I) for {κ0, κ1, κ2} = {1, 0.3, 0.04}, γ = 0.4, σ = +1, and ωp = 0. The pump and seed amplitudes are Ap = 0.24 and As = 0.11. Left: initial (red dashed) and output (blue) temporal amplitude profiles; the inset shows propagation. Right: corresponding spectra in the numerical coordinate Ω= −ω. The phase-matched idler grows while the packets separate according to their group velocities.

FIG. 5. Configuration (I) with the parameters of Fig. 4 except ωp = −3.75. The substantially different group velocities produce a much larger temporal displacement. The spectral coordinate is Ω= −ω, so the pump appears near Ω= 3.75.
